clue.text: Report from Helsinki River Meadows, wicked Deb’s alma mater?

indicators.note: a report is something spoken and heard, so the words that follow count for their sound rather than their spelling

blocks.note: someone from Helsinki is Finnish, which is said the same as the word for completing
ings are low-lying meadows beside a river, a northern English dialect word
wicked and cool are both slang for excellent; spoken after the S of the meadows they run on as the end of an educational establishment

explanation.surface: A dispatch from Finland about some riverside fields and a naughty debutante's former college.
explanation.walkthrough: Said aloud, 'Finnish ings cool' runs together as FINISHING SCHOOL. 'River Meadows' looks like a place name in the report, but ings is a dialect word for such meadows.
explanation.definitionFit: Debutantes were traditionally sent to private establishments teaching social graces before entering society, so it is where such a girl was educated.

clue.text: Separate pieces in this great ship, having Joplin & co supported by crewman

definitions.note: describes the condition rather than naming it: a state in which things lie in separate pieces

indicators.note: to have something is to hold it, so the outer word takes the other letters within it
in a down entry something supported sits above whatever holds it up, fixing the order of two pieces

blocks.note: fine as in splendid or excellent
SS is the abbreviation for steamship
Scott Joplin and his fellow composers of ragtime pieces could be called rag men
a tar is a sailor

explanation.surface: A musical company aboard a grand liner, with Janis Joplin's band propped up by a deckhand, seems to be falling apart.
explanation.walkthrough: Joplin suggests the singer Janis, but it is Scott Joplin, king of ragtime, whose pieces were rags. 'Great ship' splits around the musicians and the sailor.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun names the quality of existing only as broken bits, which is exactly a condition where everything lies around in disconnected parts.

clue.text: An inventory missing first and last fruit

indicators.note: missing means lacking, so the opening letter of the whole and its closing letter are dropped

blocks.note: an means one, as in 'an apple' or 'one apple'
an inventory is a list of goods

explanation.surface: A stocktake has lost the first and last items of fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: The first letter of ONE and the last of LIST go, leaving NE and LIS. 'An inventory' looks like one phrase but is two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Nelis is a variety of winter pear, so it is a specific example of that kind of produce.

clue.text: Division prepared to arrest Feds

indicators.note: arresting someone means taking them into custody, so one piece holds the other inside it

blocks.note: set means ready or prepared
G-men are FBI agents, known as Feds

explanation.surface: A police division is ready to arrest federal agents.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface has the Feds being arrested, and in the wordplay they are: G-men, American slang for FBI agents, sit inside SET.
explanation.definitionFit: A segment is one of the portions something is split into, so it is a synonym for a part or section.

clue.text: Drifter from pack runs cop out of corrupt police force

indicators.note: out of means taken away from, so these letters are subtracted from the longer phrase
corrupt means spoilt or altered, so the remaining letters are put into a different order

blocks.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for runs
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A drifter from a gang has run off, leaving a policeman out of a bent force.
explanation.walkthrough: Take R and C, O, P out of POLICE FORCE and LIEFOCE remains to be rearranged. 'Drifter' suggests a vagrant, but here it is something floating.
explanation.definitionFit: Pack ice breaks into sheets of frozen sea that float with the current, so one such sheet is something that drifts away from the pack.

clue.text: Artillerymen came to accept weird Scots out of love

indicators.note: to accept something is to take it in, so one piece is placed inside another
love is zero in tennis, a round letter, and being out of it means that letter is dropped

blocks.note: came to (like) and grew to (like) mean the same; 'to' does double work as part of the phrase
unco is a Scots word for strange or weird

explanation.surface: Gunners grudgingly came round to some odd Scotsmen, though they were no longer in love.
explanation.walkthrough: UNCO loses its O (love = nil in tennis) and the remaining UNC is taken into GREW.
explanation.definitionFit: A gun crew is the team of soldiers serving a single artillery piece, so they are gunners collectively.

clue.text: Song about rebellious agent in what’s central to plot

indicators.note: rebels turn against authority, so this word is turned back to front
central means at the middle, so only the letters at the centre of the next word are kept
in means placed inside, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: CA is short for circa, about
a spy is a secret agent
the middle two letters of the word

explanation.surface: A ballad about a rebel agent who sits at the heart of a conspiracy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plot' looks like the conspiracy, but only its middle two letters are used, wrapped around the backwards agent; 'about' here is the Latin abbreviation for circa.
explanation.definitionFit: A calypso is a type of Caribbean ballad, often topical and satirical, so it is an example of the general word.

clue.text: Showing player ignoring answer in a row

indicators.note: ignoring something means leaving it out, so a letter is omitted

blocks.note: a film that is showing is on
a thespian is an actor or player
A is the abbreviation for answer

explanation.surface: An actor appears on screen, but the one taking part pays no attention to a reply in a quarrel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a row' looks like a quarrel but means one after another. THESPIAN drops its A.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'three wins on the spin' means consecutively, matching the phrase for successive occurrences.

clue.text: Fail mentally, as did historical curator of the Parthenon?

definitions.text: as did historical curator of the Parthenon?

blocks.note: first meaning: an idiom for going mad

blocks.clueFragment: as did historical curator of the Parthenon?
blocks.note: second meaning: Greece, keeper of the temple, had its sculptures removed to London by Lord Elgin

explanation.surface: Someone cracks up, just as the Parthenon's old custodian did.
explanation.walkthrough: The Elgin Marbles were carved friezes taken from the Parthenon in Athens by Lord Elgin and now in the British Museum, so its keeper literally lost them; fittingly, the setter is Elgar.
explanation.definitionFit: Marbles is slang for one's wits or sanity, so to be without them is an idiom for becoming irrational or crazy.

clue.text: Curse analogue reprogramming after power cuts

indicators.note: reprogramming rewrites things in a new configuration, so the letters are rearranged
something that cuts into a word goes inside it, splitting it

blocks.note: taken as written
P is the abbreviation for power

explanation.surface: Someone swears at their old analogue machines having to be reset after a blackout.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Power cuts' reads as blackouts, but power is P and it cuts into the rearranged ANALOGUE.
explanation.definitionFit: The Shakespearean imprecation 'a plague on both your houses' is the model: it wishes misfortune on someone, an imprecation.

clue.text: Sleep-inducer resembling Spooner’s Pobble?

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words, so the initial sounds here are exchanged

blocks.note: Lear's Pobble had no toes; swapping the opening sounds of the two syllables gives the plant's name

explanation.surface: Something that sends you to sleep, rather like the nonsense poem's creature as the Reverend would describe it.
explanation.walkthrough: Edward Lear's poem 'The Pobble Who Has No Toes' supplies the description, and the swap turns 'toe-less' into 'lo-tus'.
explanation.definitionFit: In Homer, eating the fruit of this plant made the Lotophagi drowsy and forgetful, so it is a classic soporific.

clue.text: Lay wrong cards, overturning one’s unusual lead with spades

indicators.note: overturning flips something over, so the letters run backwards
unusual means out of the ordinary, so the letters are not in their ordinary order

blocks.note: one's can stand for 'one is', which is I'M
taken as written
S is the card abbreviation for spades

explanation.surface: A bridge player puts down the wrong cards, turning over an odd lead in spades.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One's' must be read as 'one is', giving I'M, which is then turned round. 'Lead' looks like the card led, but it is just letters to rearrange with S.
explanation.definitionFit: To misdeal is to hand out playing cards incorrectly, so it is to distribute or put down cards in error.

clue.text: Reinforcing luxury cast iron chains

indicators.note: metal that is cast is melted and poured into a new shape, so these letters are remoulded
chains confine whatever they bind, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: a pie is a welcome treat or indulgence
taken as written

explanation.surface: A deluxe cast-iron chain sounds like heavy-duty reinforcement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cast iron' looks like a single material, but 'cast' is the instruction to rearrange IRON, which then wraps round the treat.
explanation.definitionFit: In Baroque music the ripieno players reinforce the soloists, so the musical term is an adjective meaning supplementary or filling out.

clue.text: Person addicted to MDMA

blocks.note: someone hooked on a drug is said to be on it
MDMA is the drug Ecstasy, known as E

explanation.surface: Someone hooked on a party drug.
explanation.walkthrough: MDMA is the chemical name for Ecstasy, commonly called E.
explanation.definitionFit: The pronoun stands for an unspecified individual, as in 'one never knows', so it can replace a word for an individual human.

clue.text: African orange juice emptied by topless fan over painting?

indicators.note: an emptied container has nothing inside, so only the outer letters are kept
without a top means the first letter is removed
turned over means flipped, so the letters go backwards

blocks.note: the word without its first letter
painting is a form of art
the word with its inside letters taken out

explanation.surface: A glass of fruit juice drunk dry by a half-naked admirer of a picture.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces are read in a different order from the clue: the turned-round fan comes first, then ART, then the emptied juice.
explanation.definitionFit: Naartje is the South African name for a tangerine or mandarin, a small citrus fruit grown in that country.

clue.text: In rubbish truck, inverted drawer

indicators.note: something inverted is turned upside down, which in a down entry means the letters run backwards

blocks.note: at and in are interchangeable for location, as in 'at home'
rot means nonsense or rubbish
a cart is a simple goods vehicle

explanation.surface: Someone has been tipped upside down into the back of a rubbish truck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drawer' suggests a sliding box, but it means one who draws, pulling things in.
explanation.definitionFit: To draw can mean to pull towards oneself, so something that draws things in is a magnet or anything exerting pull.

clue.text: Comedienne losing money in SA undertaking

indicators.note: losing something means no longer having it, so those letters are taken away

blocks.note: Jo Brand is a British stand-up comic
the rand is South Africa's currency

explanation.surface: A comic goes broke while working in South Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: Jo Brand is a well-known British comedian; take away the South African currency and JOB is left.
explanation.definitionFit: A job is a task or piece of work someone takes on, the sense of an enterprise or project.

clue.text: I’m thrilled band has cracked No. 1

indicators.note: to crack something is to break into it, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: number one is a nursery euphemism for urination, a wee
a hoop is a circular band

explanation.surface: A delighted musician whose group has reached the top of the charts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Band' and 'No. 1' suggest a chart-topping group, but band is a hoop and No. 1 is a child's word for a wee.
explanation.definitionFit: The exclamation expresses delight, so it stands in for a phrase announcing that the speaker feels excited.

clue.text: Kept in with a donor

indicators.note: in means contained inside, so the letters lie within the following words

blocks.note: running across the end of the first word, the second word and the start of the third

explanation.surface: Someone was held on side with a benefactor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kept in with' looks like a phrase about staying friendly, but the definition stops at 'Kept'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are past tenses meaning possessed or retained, as in 'she had it' or 'she kept it'.

clue.text: Perennial violence cable television edited out

indicators.note: out means removed, so one set of letters is taken from another
edited material is reworked, so the remaining letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A perennial complaint: violent scenes cut from cable TV.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perennial' looks like an adjective about the complaint, but it is a noun for a plant. Remove the letters of VIOLENCE from CABLE TELEVISION and seven letters remain.
explanation.definitionFit: Astilbe is a garden plant with feathery flower plumes that comes back every year, so it is an example of such a plant.

clue.text: One of the chores, to cut general greenery

indicators.note: cutting into something means going inside it, so one piece is inserted

blocks.note: Robert E Lee was the Confederate general
a fag is British slang for a tiresome chore, so one of them is a fag

explanation.surface: Pruning the garden plants is one of the household tasks.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang a fag is a tedious job ('what a fag'); A FAG goes inside the general's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Leafage is foliage collectively, the leaves of plants, which is what green vegetation consists of.

clue.text: Feature academic on East London Radio?

indicators.note: radio is heard not seen, and an East London accent drops the initial H, so this is a Cockney pronunciation

blocks.note: an academic or intellectual is highbrow, and a Cockney drops the H

explanation.surface: A programme profiling a scholar on a local station in the East End.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockneys, from East London, traditionally drop their aitches, so 'highbrow' comes out as 'ighbrow'.
explanation.definitionFit: Feature can mean a part of the face such as nose, mouth or brow, and the hairy arch above the eye is one.

clue.text: Mad keen on cycling, ultimately

indicators.note: going round in a cycle moves the front letter to the back

blocks.note: taken as written
keen and fine both mean sharp, as of an edge

explanation.surface: Someone crazy about bike riding, in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cycling' suggests bikes, but it shifts the leading M of MAD FINE to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase means 'to the end' or 'towards the conclusion', the same idea as finally or at the last.

clue.text: Real name 24 Across heard adopted by a gangster played by Al P?

indicators.note: heard means listened to, so the cross-referenced word counts by its sound
an adopted child is taken into a family, so one piece is taken inside another

blocks.note: the answer to 24 across is said like the letter
taken as written
Al Pacino played Tony Montana in Scarface; the name is shortened just as Al P is

explanation.surface: Asking a mobster's true identity, as played by a famous actor.
explanation.walkthrough: Al P is Al Pacino, shortened, and the question mark signals that the mobster's surname is shortened in the same way to its initial.
explanation.definitionFit: An autonym is the name a person actually bears, as opposed to a pseudonym, so it is the genuine name.

clue.text: If dry, a southern outing once a week

indicators.note: an outing takes things out of their usual place, so the letters are moved around

blocks.note: taken as written
S is the abbreviation for southern

explanation.surface: If the weather stays fine, there is a weekly trip south.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outing' looks like a trip, but it is the instruction to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Used adverbially, as in 'open Fridays', it means on every such weekday, which happens weekly.

clue.text: Boundaries being pushed by our Toughie solvers

indicators.note: if the boundaries are pushed out, the edges go and only the interior of the phrase is kept

blocks.note: the two words without their first and last letters

explanation.surface: The setter congratulates readers who stretch the limits of what they can solve.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pushing boundaries' sounds like ambition, but here it means pushing them away.
explanation.definitionFit: The setter addresses readers directly, so the second-person pronoun stands for the people tackling this puzzle.

clue.text: Small short measure takes nothing out

indicators.note: short means lacking, so the following letter is missing from the word
to take something in is to hold it, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for small
size is a measure of magnitude
nada is Spanish for nothing, also used in American English

explanation.surface: A short measure of drink leaves someone with nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Small short measure' looks like one phrase but means SIZE short of S. 'Out' looks like part of 'takes out', but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Out can mean unconscious or not fully alert, and being dazed is that stupefied, stunned state.

clue.text: 1960s dance fan who wants another card?

blocks.note: first meaning: a devotee of the Twist, the dance craze of the early sixties
second meaning: in pontoon a player asking for one more card says 'twist'

explanation.surface: A sixties dancer who is also a card player always asking for more.
explanation.walkthrough: Pontoon is the British version of blackjack, where 'twist' means take another card and 'stick' means stop.
explanation.definitionFit: Adding the agent ending to the dance's name, or to the card-game call, gives a word for someone doing either.

clue.text: Detective leaves Iraola’s men a word of comfort

indicators.note: when someone leaves, they are no longer present, so those letters are removed

blocks.note: DS is a Detective Sergeant
Andoni Iraola manages Liverpool Football Club, nicknamed the Reds

explanation.surface: A detective walks away from a football squad with a few consoling words.
explanation.walkthrough: Liverpool FC are known as the Reds; take away DS, Detective Sergeant.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying 'there, there' is the traditional way to soothe someone upset, so the word works as consolation.

clue.text: In time with Twitter's successor, punters essentially say “bye”

indicators.note: the essence of something is its core, so the central letter is taken
in means placed within, so the letters go inside another word

blocks.note: an era is a period of time
Twitter was renamed X
the middle letter of the seven

explanation.surface: Gamblers say goodbye to the social media platform now it has been renamed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bye' looks like a farewell, but in cricket it is a run scored when the ball passes the batter and keeper, one of the runs not credited to a batter.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket byes are counted among the extras, the runs added to the total without coming off the bat, so a bye is an example.

clue.text: “Curious Belgian cracks case of reprisal” – sound familiar?

indicators.note: curious means odd or strange, so the letters appear in a strange order
to crack something open is to break into it, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: taken as written
the case of a word is its outer letters

explanation.surface: A headline about Poirot, the inquisitive Belgian detective, solving a revenge case; does that remind you of anything?
explanation.walkthrough: The surface evokes Hercule Poirot cracking a case, but 'case' means the outer letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'that rings a bell' means something seems vaguely familiar, as if prompting memory.

clue.text: No man, it's said, can crew for ketch and schooner?

blocks.note: first meaning: the biblical saying that nobody can owe loyalty to opposing lords at once
second meaning: to crew is to work on board, and a ketch and a schooner each have a pair of masts

explanation.surface: A proverb seems to say nobody can sail on two different boats at once.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'master' here is a two-master, a vessel with two masts. The italic 'and' stresses both ships at once.
explanation.definitionFit: The Gospel saying is 'No man can serve two masters', and crewing aboard a two-masted vessel is a literal version.
